content.text:
**Short answer: probably not “obviously undervalued” after its huge run, but it may still be strategically attractive if you’re buying it as insurance rather than as a cheap asset.**

Gold is hard to value because it has **no cash flows**—no earnings, coupon, or dividend—so “undervalued” depends on what you compare it to: real interest rates, the dollar, inflation risk, central-bank demand, geopolitical risk, and portfolio diversification.

### Why gold may **not** be undervalued
- **Price already reflects a lot of good news.** Gold reportedly surged about **30% in 2024** and around **60% in 2025**, then moved sideways in 2026 after trading above **$5,000/oz** in mid-March and under **$4,500/oz** recently. That suggests the market has already priced in a large amount of demand, rate-cut expectations, and geopolitical risk. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/05/gold-dollar-central-banks-risk?utm_source=openai))  
- **It is not cheap versus recent history.** Record or near-record prices don’t automatically mean overvalued, but they do reduce the margin of safety.
- **If real yields rise or the dollar strengthens, gold can struggle.** Because gold pays no income, higher real rates increase the opportunity cost of holding it.

### Why gold may still be **fairly valued or undervalued structurally**
- **Central-bank demand remains strong.** The World Gold Council reported estimated net central-bank purchases of **244 tonnes in Q1 2026**, describing activity as still elevated. ([gold.org](https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-demand-trends/gold-demand-trends-q1-2026/central-banks?utm_source=openai))  
- **Investment demand has broadened.** Physically backed gold ETFs saw positive Q1 2026 demand, with holdings increasing by **62 tonnes**, according to the World Gold Council. ([gold.org](https://www.gold.org/download/file/20795/Q1_2026_GDT_Press_Release_29_April.pdf?utm_source=openai))  
- **Macro conditions can still support gold.** The World Gold Council’s 2026 outlook says the current price broadly reflects consensus expectations, but softer growth, easier policy, and geopolitical risks are more likely to support gold than undermine it. ([gold.org](https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-outlook-2026?utm_source=openai))  
- **Reserve diversification is a real long-term theme.** Gold has gained importance in central-bank reserves, though dollar assets still remain the largest reserve category. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/06/05/gold-dollar-central-banks-risk?utm_source=openai))  

### My take
If by **undervalued** you mean “priced below intrinsic value like a stock,” I’d say **no clear evidence**—gold looks closer to **fairly valued to somewhat rich** after a major rally.

If by **undervalued** you mean “under-owned relative to long-term monetary, geopolitical, and debt risks,” then **possibly yes**, especially for investors with little or no gold exposure.

A reasonable framing:

| Investor goal | View on gold |
|---|---|
| Short-term trade | Not obviously cheap; vulnerable to pullbacks |
| Inflation / currency hedge | Still useful |
| Portfolio insurance | Reasonable, especially at 5–10% allocation |
| Aggressive return asset | Less compelling after the rally |
| Long-term fiat-risk hedge | Still defensible |

**Bottom line:** I wouldn’t call gold a screaming bargain today. I’d call it a **reasonable hedge at a not-cheap price**. If you already own a lot, trimming or rebalancing may make sense. If you own none, gradually building a modest allocation could still be rational.
